title: Zacchaeus
note:
Primary, Chapter 3, from the Mar Thoma Sunday School Samajam Primary Vol-1, pages 17–20. The first chapter in this library that is not a Beginner’s, and the first written to a band above the youngest — so the whole of it is calibrated one rung up: four options where Beginner gets three, a six-step sequence where Beginner gets four, wrong answers that are true sentences about the same story rather than obviously wrong ones, and a memory verse practice that begins where Beginner’s ends.

That last point is not a figure of speech. St. Luke 19: 10 is also the memory verse of Beginner Chapter 3, The Lost Coin, so the two classes can be laid side by side on the same words — which is exactly what was done, and is why the agent’s own Primary rung was set aside here. See the verse note.

Games from the Game Builder agent (`npm run agent:games -- --class primary --chapter 03`): the planner read the three curriculum questions, classified them attributes / cause / identity, and assigned reveal, multiple-choice and match. Those three are its work. The fourth and fifth are added by hand because three questions is below the Primary band’s four-to-five, and padding the three into five would have been the worse answer; what they cover is written in their notes.

Artwork downloaded from Drive (Primary / Chapter 03 / 04 - Story Artwork) and read panel by panel before a word of alt text was written; PNG to WebP at native size, no resize and no crop. Seventeen files: a portrait cover, a landscape cover and fifteen panels. Panels 6, 7 and 8 are 941×1671, 941×1671 and 942×1670 rather than the canonical 941×1672 — one or two pixels, converted without distortion and recorded rather than silently fixed.

The artwork brought a frame the draft did not have. It opens on a boy in a present-day market who cannot see over the crowd (panels 1–3), tells Zacchaeus (4–12), and returns to the same boy (13–15), where Halo asks him what he can do when he makes a wrong choice and the last panel answers it. So the eighteen text cards written before the artwork arrived are gone, replaced by the fifteen panels the chapter actually has; the narration is lettered into the art, so no card carries `text` and every alt quotes the words painted on its own panel.

One copy warning is left standing on purpose: the verse practice’s gap-fill prompt is the verse itself with a hole in it, and shortening it would mean altering the verse. Where a budget and a quotation disagree the quotation wins, and the budget reports it rather than being widened to hide it.

The book spells the name “Zacchaeus” throughout the lesson and “Zaccheus” once, in the last sentence of p.18. The artwork spells it “Zacchaeus” everywhere, which is the spelling used here.

cover.note: Chapter 3’s own cover, drawn twice. The portrait is 941×1672 with “3” and “ZACCHAEUS” painted into it, so the story reader lays no text over it. The landscape is the same scene at 1672×941 and carries no title, which is what the two screens that crop a cover actually need — the chapter hub and the shelf row both draw their own heading, and both were throwing most of the portrait away to fit a wide box. Zacchaeus leans out of the sycamore-fig at the left and Jesus, in the street below, reaches up towards him; Jericho’s walls and market stand behind. Same moment, same characters, two crops of one picture — never two different covers, or a child meets one on the shelf and another inside.

story.alt: A crowded street market in bright sun — fruit stalls, bunting, a stage far off with musicians on it. A small boy in a blue T-shirt and backpack stands hemmed in by grown-ups, one hand on a man's back, craning up. Halo glows beside his shoulder. The boy says, “I can’t see!” A chalkboard behind him reads “Good Food Brighter Days”.
story.note: The chapter does not open in Jericho. The artwork frames the lesson with a boy in a present-day market who cannot see over the crowd — panels 1 to 3 — goes to Zacchaeus in panels 4 to 12, and comes back to the same boy in panels 13 to 15, where the lesson lands as something he can do. That frame is the artwork’s, not an invention here, and it is the same shape Beginner Chapter 5 turned out to have.

story.alt: The same market. The boy has turned round, chin resting on his fist, thinking. Halo floats by the mango baskets and asks, “What could you do?” Just past his shoulder a hand-painted sign on the pavement reads “Better View This Way!” with an arrow.

The boy has climbed onto a low stone wall, hands on the edge, and now he can see the stage over everyone’s heads. He is beaming. Halo, above him, says, “Someone in the Bible wanted to see Jesus like this too.”

A narration box reads, “Zacchaeus lived in Jericho. He was a chief tax collector and a wealthy man. One day, he heard that Jesus was passing through the city.” Zacchaeus sits at a tax table in a dark red robe and embroidered cap, a pen in his ringed hand, stacks of coins, scales and money chests in front of him. A cloth sign above reads “TAX COLLECTION” over a pair of scales. In the street beyond, a man throws up an arm and calls, “Jesus is passing through Jericho!” Halo hovers at the stall.

“But there was a big crowd, and Zacchaeus was too short to see over the people.” We are behind Zacchaeus in the crowd: shoulders and turbans tower over him on every side, his hands pressed against two backs, his face tilted up. Far down the street, small between the heads, Jesus walks towards the city gate.

“Zacchaeus was determined to see Jesus. He ran ahead of the crowd and climbed up a sycamore-fig tree.” Zacchaeus is halfway up a broad, rough-barked trunk, one sandal braced on a low wall, robe swinging, both hands gripping the bark. Below and behind him the crowd streams on towards the gate without him.

“He sat on a branch, looking out for Jesus who would pass below.” Seen from up in the leaves: Zacchaeus sits astride a thick branch, looking down into the street. Jesus is walking through the middle of the crowd below, clearly visible now, people on every side of him.

“Suddenly, Jesus looked up at Zacchaeus.” Jesus stands in the street with one hand raised towards the tree, face turned up and smiling. Zacchaeus leans out along the branch above, eyes wide, caught. Jesus says, “Zacchaeus, come down immediately. I must stay at your house today.”

“Zacchaeus came down at once and gladly welcomed Jesus to his home.” The two walk side by side along a sunlit street, Zacchaeus half a step ahead with one arm flung out towards his doorway, looking up at Jesus and talking. The crowd follows behind them, smiling.

“Zacchaeus was overjoyed. After his encounter with Jesus, he was transformed.” Inside the house: Jesus sits on a cushioned bench, Zacchaeus stands before him with both hands clasped at his chest. Shelves of chests, coins and brass vessels line the wall behind, and a low table is set with fruit.

“Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, ‘Look, Lord! Here and now, I give half of my possessions to the poor.’” Zacchaeus stands with one hand on his chest and the other open in front of him, speaking. Jesus sits listening, and the backs of several seated guests fill the foreground.

“‘And if I have cheated anybody out of anything, I will pay back four times the amount.’” Zacchaeus holds out a cloth money pouch with both hands to a seated man, who reaches up to take it. Zacchaeus says, “I will pay back four times the amount.” Jesus stands smiling behind him.

Back in the market. The boy sits on a stone block, chin on his fist, looking up. In a thought cloud above him, Zacchaeus stands with his hands clasped, facing Jesus. The narration reads, “Meeting Jesus changed Zacchaeus. He wanted to make things right.” Halo asks, “What do you think changed Zacchaeus?” A chalkboard beside him reads “Kind People Brighter Places”.

“Zacchaeus showed that he was sorry by choosing to make things right.” The boy is still thinking. Three thought clouds float above him, each with a small scene and a label: “Take something that isn’t mine”, “Hurt a friend’s feelings”, and “Tell a lie”. Halo asks, “What can you do when you make a wrong choice?” A sign nearby reads “Be Kind Be Honest Be Brave”.

interaction.prompt: What can you do when you make a wrong choice?
interaction.hint: Zacchaeus did not only feel sorry. He did something.

options.label: Say sorry and make it right

interaction.note: Halo asks this question in the artwork itself and panel 15 answers it, so the question is the page’s own and not one added on top of it. Ungated: a child who would rather turn the page may. The three wrong options are the three easy ways out of an apology, which is what makes them worth naming out loud.

story.alt: “When we make a wrong choice, we can say sorry and try to make things right.” The boy stands with his palms pressed together in apology in front of another boy who sits on a step with his arms round his knees, looking up at him. A red toy car lies on the cobbles between them. Halo says, “You can make things right, too.” A banner behind reads “A Better You A Brighter Tomorrow”.

curriculum.source: Primary Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 03 “ZACCHAEUS”, p.19 — “ANSWER THE QUESTIONS”
curriculum.note:
The three questions the Primary book prints at the end of the chapter, transcribed from the curriculum photographs in 01 - Curriculum Source and left exactly as printed — including “mee” in question 2, which is the book’s own typo and is not corrected here. Three is all the book asks; the Primary band wants four to five games, so the fourth and fifth cover the part of the lesson the question set leaves out (what Zacchaeus did afterwards, and the closing teaching on p.19) and say so in their own notes.

The page carries the teacher’s own answer key in blue pen: ① brackets the sinner/taxing sentences, ② underlines “there was a big crowd and Zacchaeus being of short stature could not get a glimpse of Him”, and ③ underlines “sycamore-fig tree”. Each `answer` below is the sentence that mark points at, quoted from p.18 rather than reasoned out, so this block records what the curriculum says and never a second opinion about it.

questions.question: What were the shortcomings of Zacchaeus?
questions.objective: Name the two things the lesson holds against him: he was considered a sinner, and he was believed to have grown rich by taxing people as he wanted.
questions.answer: “He was considered a sinner by the people, as it was believed that Zacchaeus had become rich by using his position to tax people as he wanted. This made the people resentful of this man who was cheating them.” (p.18)
questions.note: Marked ① on the page. The lesson gives this as what people *believed* about him, and the game keeps that framing rather than upgrading it to a verdict.

questions.question: Why was it difficult for Zacchaeus to mee Jesus?
questions.objective: Hold both causes at once — a big crowd, and his own short stature. Neither one alone is the answer the lesson gives.
questions.answer: “However, there was a big crowd and Zacchaeus being of short stature could not get a glimpse of Him.” (p.18)
questions.note: Marked ② on the page. “mee” is printed in the book; it is not a typo introduced here.

questions.question: Which tree did Zacchaeus climb to see Jesus?
questions.objective: Name the sycamore-fig tree, and know why he climbed it — he ran ahead of the crowd to see Jesus pass below.
questions.answer: “He ran ahead of the crowd and climbed up a sycamore-fig tree. He sat on a branch, looking out for Jesus who would pass below.” (p.18)

games.title: What They Held Against Him
games.objective: Name the two things the lesson holds against Zacchaeus — that he was considered a sinner, and that he was believed to have grown rich by taxing people as he wanted.
games.note: Question 1. A reveal rather than a quiz, because “what were his shortcomings” has more than one answer and a question with one right box teaches the opposite. Nothing here is correct or incorrect; four cards are turned over and each one says what the lesson says. The fourth is the consequence rather than a shortcoming, and it is included because the lesson gives it in the same breath. The prompt says tap rather than turn over: these cards carry words and nothing is hidden behind them, so “turn over” promised a flip the screen never performs. Shelf picture: the tax table in panel 4, with the scales, the coin stacks and the “TAX COLLECTION” sign — the only panel that shows the job and the wealth this game is about. The cards themselves stay words: three of the four have nothing drawn for them, and illustrating one of four is a hint, not artwork.

interactions.prompt: Tap each thing the people said about him.

games.title: Why He Could Not See
games.objective: Hold both causes at once: the crowd was big and Zacchaeus was short. Either one on its own is only half the lesson's answer.
games.note:
Question 2. The lesson gives one sentence with two causes in it, and the two wrong options are each exactly half of that sentence — a child who remembers only the crowd, or only his height, finds an option waiting for them and has to notice it is short of the answer. Nothing in the labels flags which is which. The fourth is a thing that never happened. Four options is the Primary band’s ceiling; Beginner’s is three.

Shelf picture: panel 5, which is this question drawn — the view from behind Zacchaeus with the crowd towering over him and Jesus tiny in the distance. It shows both causes at once and names neither, which is exactly what the shelf should do.

interactions.prompt: Why could Zacchaeus not see Jesus?
interactions.hint: The lesson gives two reasons in one sentence, not one.

options.label: The crowd, and his short stature

games.title: The Tree He Climbed
games.objective: Name the sycamore-fig tree, and know why he climbed it — to see Jesus pass below, not to hide, rest or pick fruit.
games.note:
Question 3, in two halves: the match names the things in the story, and the choice that follows asks the *why* the question’s objective also wants. Both wrong options in the choice are true sentences about this story — he did sit on a branch, and it was a fig tree — which makes the question “which of these was the reason” rather than “which of these happened”. That is the discrimination Primary is for.

Shelf picture: panel 6, the climb. The pairs stay words on purpose — putting the tree’s picture on the “Sycamore-fig” card would let a child match it to “The tree he climbed” without reading either, which is the opposite of what a matching game is for.

interactions.prompt: Match each one to what it was.
interactions.hint: One of them is the tree.
He ran ahead so he could see Jesus pass below.

games.title: What Happened That Day
games.objective: Put the day in order, from hearing that Jesus was near to paying back what he took.
games.note:
The book asks three questions and the Primary band wants four to five games, so this one covers what the questions leave out: the shape of the day. Six steps, because the band’s own note says a sequence may run longer than four here, and because six is what the lesson actually has. It answers no curriculum question and is not pretending to.

Every step is one of the chapter’s own panels, in the order the artwork tells it — the tax table, the crowd, the climb, Jesus looking up, the walk home, the money paid back. This is the one game the artwork changed outright: it was six text cards before the panels arrived, and ordering pictures is what this mechanic wanted all along. The labels stay as captions so a child who reads gets both.

Shelf picture named rather than left to fall out of the game: without it the shelf takes the first picture the game uses, which is panel 4 — already game 1’s card, so two of the five rows were the same tax table. Panel 9, the walk home, is this game’s own middle and belongs to no other card.

interactions.hint: It starts before he ever saw Jesus.

games.title: True or Not?
games.objective: Test what the lesson actually says against what it is easy to assume — including its closing teaching, that Jesus can see you wherever you are.
games.note: The fifth game, and the only one that reaches past the story into the lesson’s own closing paragraph on p.19. Every false statement carries its reason immediately after it, so nothing untrue is ever left standing on the screen. The reasons are the lesson’s own sentences rather than a commentary on them. Shelf picture: panel 10, Zacchaeus standing in his own house with his hands clasped — the moment the lesson calls transformed, which is what most of these statements circle.

interactions.prompt: Say what you think. Then we will look.

statements.source: Zacchaeus was a poor man with nothing of his own.
statements.because: No. He was a chief tax collector, and the lesson calls him a wealthy man.

statements.source: Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus.
statements.because: Yes. He ran ahead of the crowd and climbed up a sycamore-fig tree.

statements.source: Jesus walked past and would not go to his house.
statements.because: No. Jesus looked up and said He must stay at his house that day.

statements.source: After meeting Jesus, Zacchaeus kept everything he had.
statements.because: No. He gave half of his possessions to the poor, and promised to pay back four times what he had taken.

statements.source: Jesus can see you wherever you are.
statements.ask: Can Jesus see you wherever you are?
statements.because: Yes. The lesson says Jesus is omnipresent — He is everywhere, and He can see you wherever you are.

verse.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

practice.note: Stage 1, and deliberately the whole of what a Beginner is asked for this same verse in Beginner Chapter 3. Primary starts where Beginner finishes.

practice.prompt: For the Son of ______ came to seek and to save the lost.
practice.note: Stage 2, the missing word with the sentence whole on both sides of it. Four options where Beginner gets three, and every one of them a real word of this verse — nothing here invents scripture to be wrong with.

practice.prompt: For the Son of Man came to ______
practice.hint: Two things follow: seeking comes before saving.
practice.note: Stage 3, the same question with the right-hand side taken away. This is the real step up from Beginner: “save” reads perfectly well in that gap and is wrong, and the only thing that separates them is remembering the verse forwards rather than reading around a hole.

practice.hint: Start with the one who came.
practice.note: Stage 4, full reconstruction — six pieces where stage 1 had four, which is the whole of the difference between the two stages. The build checks that they spell the verse exactly.

practice.prompt: Where does our verse come from?
practice.hint: It is the last verse of this chapter's Bible portion.
practice.note: Stage 5, the reference — recognised, not typed; the Primary band does not write references yet. Three options rather than Beginner’s three different books: 19: 1 is where this chapter’s own Bible portion begins, printed on p.17, and 10: 19 is the same two numbers the other way round. The field is narrower than Beginner’s and the discrimination is much finer, which is where the difficulty moved to.

verse.note:
Read from p.20 through the Memory Verse agent: `--fetch --source-dir` over the four curriculum photographs, the supervised read, then `--from-extraction`. Printed on the page inside quotation marks and with the space in “19: 10”, both kept as printed.

The agent’s Primary rung produced a three-piece arrange-words — “For the Son / of Man came to seek and / to save the lost.” — and it is not used, because Beginner Chapter 3 carries this exact verse as a four-piece arrange-words and a Primary child would have met an easier task than a Beginner. That is the one thing this ladder must never do. What ships instead is five stages that start at Beginner’s ceiling and climb: the agent’s rung is the floor here, not the whole of it. Translation is unresolved: p.20 does not name one, which is where every other chapter in this library stands.

Picture: panel 8, Jesus looking up into the tree and calling Zacchaeus down — the verse’s own sentence happening, rather than an illustration chosen to decorate it.

video.title: Zacchaeus
video.note:
Supplied for the Watch screen as an embed; only the eleven-character id is kept. The `si=` parameter on the pasted URL is a YouTube share token that identifies where the link came from, and it has no business travelling into a children’s app — the schema accepts the id alone, which is why it cannot. Served through youtube-nocookie.com, and nothing is embedded until a child asks to watch, so opening this chapter contacts YouTube not at all.

Picture: panel 8, Jesus looking up into the tree — the chapter’s own artwork rather than a YouTube thumbnail, which would reach a third party before the child had asked for anything.

decision.statement: I will always try to see Jesus and live according to His will.
decision.note: The curriculum’s own My Decision line from p.20, first person and unchanged.

song.note: The Song from p.20, in the Latin script the book prints it in, line for line.

prayer.text: Jesus, please forgive my sins and keep me close to you. Amen.
prayer.note: The closing Prayer from p.20, word for word. The chapter also opens with a prayer on p.17 — “Lord Jesus, who comes in search of us, give us the grace to learn about You. Amen.” — which has nowhere to go in this shape and is recorded here rather than lost.

celebration.message: Jesus came to look for us. You can make things right, too.
celebration.note: The memory verse and Halo’s own last line from panel 15, said back to the child.
